facts.statement: The study tested a spherical ultrasound device with a 17.5-mm radius using silicone models that mimicked shallow, deep, and irregular brain tumor cavities.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: The researchers used phosphate-buffered saline and 1% albumin as the fluids to help the ultrasound waves travel through the models.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: The team measured how clearly they could see small markers placed at depths of about 3 and 5 centimeters inside the models.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: The device stayed firmly in place and allowed the researchers to see the edges of the cavity in all three different model shapes.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: The markers were still visible at a depth of 5 centimeters regardless of which fluid was used.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: The depth of the target had a bigger effect on image clarity than the type of fluid used.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: CT scans were used to check that the models were shaped correctly and that the device fit properly.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: This feasibility study using artificial models showed that the spherical device can create a consistent surface for taking ultrasound images of simulated tumor cavities.
facts.subject: other

facts.statement: The authors state that testing in living subjects is needed to determine if the device is useful in real clinical settings.
facts.subject: other
